```{r build and load data, include=FALSE}

# ============================================================
# BUILD AND LOAD DATA
# ============================================================

# Check if cached file exists
if(file.exists("data/scf_filtered.rds")) {
  scf_filtered <- readRDS("data/scf_filtered.rds")
  # message("Loaded cached SCF data.")
  } else {
    # STEP 1: LOAD DATA (Creates correct survey design objects)
    year = 2022
    scf_raw <- scf_load(year, data_directory = "data/")
  
    # STEP 2: UPDATE VARIABLES (Adds derived vars safely)
    scf_filtered <- scf_update(scf_raw,
  
  # --- Outcome Variable ---
  # Ensure binary 0/1 (adjust logic if your pir40 is coded differently)
  pir40 = as.numeric(pir40 == 1), 
  pir40_label = factor(ifelse(pir40 == 1, "High Debt Burden",
                              "No High Debt Burden"),
                           levels = c("No High Debt Burden",
                                      "High Debt Burden")),
  
  # --- Demographics ---
  sex = factor(case_when(
    hhsex == 1 ~ "Male",
    hhsex == 2 ~ "Female",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ), levels = c("Male", "Female"), ordered = FALSE),
  
  age_group = factor(case_when(
    age >= 18 & age <= 29 ~ "18-29",
    age >= 30 & age <= 39 ~ "30-39",
    age >= 40 & age <= 49 ~ "40-49",
    age >= 50 & age <= 59 ~ "50-59",
    age >= 60 & age <= 69 ~ "60-69",
    age >= 70 ~ "70+",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ), levels = c("18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70+"), 
     ordered = FALSE),
  
  race_label = factor(case_when(
    race == 1 ~ "White non-Hispanic",
    race == 2 ~ "Black/African American",
    race == 3 ~ "Hispanic",
    race == 4 ~ "Asian/Pacific Islander",
    race == 5 ~ "Other",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ), levels = c("White non-Hispanic", "Black/African American", 
                "Hispanic", "Asian/Pacific Islander", "Other"), 
     ordered = FALSE),
  
  # --- Family Structure ---
  married_factor = factor(married,
                          levels = c(1, 2),
                          labels = c("Married", "Not Married"),
                          ordered = FALSE),
  
  married_detailed = case_when(
        x8023 == 1 ~ "Married",
        x8023 == 2 ~ "Cohabitating",
        x8023 == 3 ~ "Separated",
        x8023 == 4 ~ "Divorced",
        x8023 == 5 ~ "Widowed",
        x8023 == 6 ~ "Never Married",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
        ) %>% 
        factor(
          levels = c("Married", "Cohabitating", 
                     "Separated", "Divorced", 
                     "Widowed", "Never Married"),
          ordered = FALSE
          ),
  
  has_children = factor(kids > 0,
                        levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                        labels = c("No Children", "Has Children"),
                        ordered = FALSE),
  
  # --- Socioeconomic ---
  educ_cat = factor(case_when(
    educ %in% -1:7 ~ "Less than High School",
    educ == 8 ~ "High School Graduate",
    educ == 9 ~ "Some College",
    educ %in% 10:11 ~ "Associate's Degree",
    educ %in% 12:14 ~ "Bachelor's Degree or Higher",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ), levels = c("Less than High School", "High School Graduate", 
                "Some College", "Associate's Degree", "Bachelor's Degree or Higher"), 
     ordered = FALSE),
  
  wealth_group = factor(case_when(
    nwcat == 1 ~ "Bottom 25%",
    nwcat == 2 ~ "25–50%", 
    nwcat == 3 ~ "50–75%",
    nwcat == 4 ~ "75–90%",
    nwcat == 5 ~ "Top 10%"
  ), levels = c("Bottom 25%", "25–50%", "50–75%", "75–90%", "Top 10%"), 
     ordered = FALSE),
  
  homeownership = factor(housecl,
                         levels = c(1, 2),
                         labels = c("Homeowner", "Renter"),
                         ordered = FALSE)
  )
    saveRDS(scf_filtered, "data/scf_filtered_updated.rds")
    # message("Created and saved cached SCF data.")
  }

# Verify variables were created

c("pir40", "age", "sex", "married_factor", "married", "married_detailed", "wealth_group", "has_children", "housecl", "homeownership", "race_label", "pir40_label") %in% names(scf_filtered$mi_design[[1]]$variables)

```


Raw data suggests White households face the highest debt burden rates, but controlling for wealth reveals a stark reversal. After adjusting for socioeconomic factors, Black, Hispanic, and Asian households face 74 to 178 percent higher odds of financial distress than White households. This reveals that structural barriers, rather than individual choices, drive debt concentration among asset-poor minority families.

# Context

This analysis uses the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), a triennial survey conducted by the Federal Reserve. The sample includes approximately 5,200 U.S. households, representing the civilian noninstitutionalized population. The primary outcome is high debt burden, defined as a Payment-to-Income Ratio (PIR) exceeding 40 percent, the Federal Reserve’s standard threshold for financial distress. Key predictors include race, wealth group, education, age, marital status, and homeownership. All estimates account for the complex survey design using replicate weights and multiple imputation. This associational analysis isolates the independent relationship between race and debt burden while holding measurable economic resources constant, testing whether disparities persist beyond compositional differences.

# Findings

```{r visualizations, echo=FALSE}
# ============================================================
# PREPARE DATA FOR RACE PLOT (Self-Contained for Snapshot)
# ============================================================
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load cached results if not already in the snapshot's memory
if (!exists("race_data")) {
  biv_cache <- readRDS("results/bivariate_analysis.rds")
  race_data <- biv_cache$race_data
}

if (!exists("results_df")) {
  reg_cache <- readRDS("results/regression_analysis.rds")
  results_df <- reg_cache$results_df
}

# 2. Extract Bivariate Rates safely
race_biv <- race_data %>%
  select(Race = Race_Ethnicity, Bivariate_Rate = Percent_High_Burden)

# 3. Extract Adjusted ORs safely (Avoid brittle row indices like 19:22)
# We dynamically filter for the race variables by name
race_reg <- results_df %>%
  filter(grepl("race_label", term)) %>%
  mutate(Race = sub("race_label", "", term)) %>%
  select(Race, Adjusted_OR = estimate)

# Add the reference group (White non-Hispanic) with an OR of 1.00
race_or <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(Race = "White non-Hispanic", Adjusted_OR = 1.00),
  race_reg
) %>%
  mutate(Adjusted_OR = round(Adjusted_OR, 2))

# 4. Merge and format for plotting
race_comparison <- left_join(race_biv, race_or, by = "Race") %>%
  mutate(
    Race = factor(Race, 
                  levels = c("White non-Hispanic", "Black/African American", 
                             "Hispanic", "Asian/Pacific Islander", "Other"))
  )

# Reshape data for ggplot faceting
race_plot_data <- race_comparison %>%
  select(Race, Bivariate_Rate, Adjusted_OR) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Bivariate_Rate, Adjusted_OR), 
               names_to = "Measure", 
               values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(
    Measure = case_when(
      Measure == "Bivariate_Rate" ~ "% with High Debt Burden\n(Bivariate)",
      Measure == "Adjusted_OR" ~ "Odds Ratio\n(Adjusted)"
    ),
    Race = factor(Race, 
                  levels = c("White non-Hispanic", "Black/African American", 
                             "Hispanic", "Asian/Pacific Islander", "Other"))
  )

# Create separate data for the reference line (ONLY for Adjusted panel)
reference_line_data <- data.frame(
  Measure = "Odds Ratio\n(Adjusted)",
  yintercept = 1,
  legend_label = "Reference (OR = 1)"
)

# ============================================================
# CREATE THE RACE PLOT (Optimized for 1-Page Snapshot)
# ============================================================
race_plot <- ggplot(race_plot_data, aes(x = Race, y = Value, fill = Measure)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(data = reference_line_data, 
             aes(yintercept = yintercept, linetype = legend_label),  
             color = "#333333", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "", 
                    values = c("% with High Debt Burden\n(Bivariate)" = "#0066cc",
                               "Odds Ratio\n(Adjusted)" = "#cc3311")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "", 
                        values = c("Reference (OR = 1)" = "dashed"),
                        guide = guide_legend(
                          override.aes = list(
                            color = "#333333", 
                            fill = NA,
                            size = 1
                          )
                        )) +
  labs(title = "Racial Disparities: Raw Rates vs. Adjusted Odds",
       subtitle = "Left: Bivariate percentages | Right: Regression odds ratios",
       x = "", y = "") +
  facet_wrap(~Measure, scales = "free_y") +
  # Slightly reduced base_size and tighter margins to ensure it fits on one page
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "horizontal",
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.spacing.x = unit(0.5, "cm"),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 5),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.6, "cm"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "#333333"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9, vjust = 1),
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 5) 
  )

# Save specifically for the snapshot layout
ggsave("figures/snapshot_race_plot.png", 
       race_plot, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```


The data reveal a striking divergence between raw percentages and adjusted realities. In simple comparisons, White non-Hispanic households appear most burdened, with 11.6 percent exceeding the 40 percent PIR threshold, compared to 5.3 to 9.6 percent for minority groups. Homeowners also appear more burdened (8.5 percent) than renters (2.8 percent). However, these raw patterns mask underlying structural risks because White households are overrepresented in high-wealth groups, and homeownership mechanically increases debt payments via mortgages.

When comparing households with similar wealth, education, and family structures, the narrative flips. Asian households face the highest adjusted odds of high debt burden, at nearly three times the rate of White households. Hispanic and Black households face approximately 90 percent and 74 percent higher odds, respectively. To anchor this scale, a household in the bottom wealth quartile is more than three times as likely to experience high debt burden as a household in the top decile.

Wealth provides a strong, monotonic protective effect. Households in the top 10 percent of the wealth distribution have 75 percent lower odds of high debt burden compared to those in the bottom 25 percent. Notably, factors often assumed to drive financial stability, such as higher education or middle age, do not independently reduce debt burden once race and wealth are accounted for. A college degree does not shield minority households from racialized credit markets.

Ultimately, debt circulates along pathways shaped by pre-existing vulnerabilities. Households without assets lack buffers against income shocks, forcing them to rely on credit to maintain basic consumption. The persistence of these disparities suggests that historical exclusion from wealth-building programs and ongoing discrimination continue to shape financial vulnerability independent of measured socioeconomic status.

# Implication

These findings suggest that interventions focused solely on financial literacy or broad-based homeownership promotion may be insufficient to reduce financial fragility. Because debt burden reflects structural barriers rather than individual deficits, policymakers may want to examine whether existing safety nets effectively reach lower-income and minority households.

The persistent adjusted disparities suggest that racially targeted debt relief and credit market reforms addressing discriminatory lending could be more effective than universal financial education campaigns. Furthermore, because wealth protection is strongest at the top of the distribution, policies may warrant a focus on helping households escape the bottom wealth quartile through robust emergency savings infrastructure. Ultimately, reducing high debt burden requires acknowledging that financial fragility is shaped by structural forces as much as individual circumstances.
